syllabus:
SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL
ECON 301 Intermediate Microeconomics - Fall 2026
Instructor: Dr. Marguerite Okonkwo-Lindqvist, Hargrove Hall 214
Email: m.okonkwo-lindqvist@example.edu
Office hours: Tue 2:00-4:00 pm, Wed 10:00-11:00 am
Meets: Tue/Thu 11:00 am-12:15 pm, Hargrove 105
Textbook: Intermediate Microeconomics: A Modern Approach (fictional course edition)
Prerequisites: ECON 101, MATH 120 (calculus I)

COURSE DESCRIPTION
This course develops the theory of consumer and producer choice and market structure using graphs and basic calculus. We start with preferences and end with monopoly and market failure.

WEEKLY SCHEDULE
Week 1 (Aug 24): Intro, constrained optimization review, budget constraints
Week 2 (Aug 31): Preferences, indifference curves, MRS
Week 3 (Sep 7): Utility functions (no class Mon Sep 7, Labor Day)
Week 4 (Sep 14): Utility maximization, corner solutions. Quiz 1 closes Sat Sep 12
Week 5 (Sep 21): Demand curves, Engel curves, elasticity
Week 6 (Sep 28): Revealed preference, cost minimization intro
Week 7 (Oct 5): Income and substitution effects. Quiz 2 closes Sat Oct 3
Week 8 (Oct 12): Slutsky equation, Giffen and inferior goods
Week 9 (Oct 19): Consumer surplus, CV and EV. Quiz 3 closes Sat Oct 24
Week 10 (Oct 26): Choice under uncertainty, risk aversion
Week 11 (Nov 2): Midterm review; MIDTERM EXAM Thu Nov 5
Week 12 (Nov 9): Production functions, returns to scale
Week 13 (Nov 16): Cost curves, short run vs long run. Quiz 4 closes Sat Nov 21
Week 14 (Nov 23): Perfect competition (no class Thu Nov 26, Thanksgiving)
Week 15 (Nov 30): Monopoly, price discrimination. Quiz 5 closes Sat Dec 5
Week 16 (Dec 7): Externalities, review
FINAL EXAM: Tue Dec 15, 10:30 am-12:30 pm, Hargrove 105

QUIZZES
Quiz 1 (Sat Sep 12): Budget constraints, preferences, MRS
Quiz 2 (Sat Oct 3): Utility maximization and demand
Quiz 3 (Sat Oct 24): Income and substitution effects, Slutsky equation
Quiz 4 (Sat Nov 21): Production and cost curves
Quiz 5 (Sat Dec 5): Perfect competition and monopoly
All quizzes are online on the course site, 30 minutes, open Friday 8:00 am and close Saturday 11:59 pm. The lowest quiz score is dropped.

EXAMS
Midterm (Thu Nov 5, in class) covers Weeks 1-10. The final (Tue Dec 15) is cumulative with extra weight on Weeks 11-16.

GRADING
Quizzes (best 4 of 5): 20%
Problem sets (6 total): 15%
Midterm exam: 25%
Final exam: 30%
Participation and clicker questions: 10%
Grade scale: A 93+, A- 90, B+ 87, B 83, B- 80, C+ 77, C 73, C- 70, D 60, F below 60.

POLICIES
1. Late work: Problem sets lose 10% per day late, and are not accepted after 3 days. Quizzes cannot be made up without documentation of illness or emergency.
2. Collaboration: You may discuss problem sets with classmates, but you must write up your own solutions and list your collaborators. Exams are closed-book; a non-graphing calculator and one handwritten sheet are allowed.
3. Accommodations: Students with approved accommodations should send their letter to the instructor by the end of Week 2 so arrangements can be made for quizzes and exams.

Schedule changes will be announced in class and on the course site.

ECON 301 - my notes (Sofia)

TOPIC 1: Utility max + budget constraint
- BC: p1x1 + p2x2 = m. slope = -p1/p2. intercepts m/p1, m/p2
- indiff curves: convex = ppl like avg bundles over extremes (diminishing MRS)
- MRS = MU1/MU2 = how much x2 ur willing to give up for 1 more x1
- OPTIMUM (interior): MRS = p1/p2 (tangency) + spend all income
- same as MU1/p1 = MU2/p2 -> bang per buck equal
- ex: u = x1*x2 (Cobb-Douglas), m=100, p1=2, p2=5 -> x1 = m/(2p1) = 25, x2 = m/(2p2) = 10. check: 2*25 + 5*10 = 100 ok
- general C-D u = x1^a x2^(1-a): x1 = a*m/p1
- corner sol: when MRS != price ratio at the boundary, spend everything on one good. happens w/ perfect substitutes (u = x1 + x2, buy whichever is cheaper) 
- perfect complements u = min(x1,x2): consume at the kink, x1=x2=m/(p1+p2)
- !! tangency isnt enough if curves non-convex, check 2nd order

TOPIC 2: Income + substitution effects
- price of x1 falls -> total effect (TE) = SE + IE
- SE: change in x1 from relative price change holding purchasing power const (Slutsky: pivot BC thru the OLD bundle)
- IE: change from the real income change
- normal good: SE and IE same direction -> demand slopes down 100%
- inferior good: IE opposite. SE is still negative for price drop (always!). if IE bigger than SE -> Giffen (rare, upward demand)
- Slutsky eq: dx1/dp1 = SE - x1 * dx1/dm
- steps for graph: 1) old bundle A on old BC 2) draw decomp BC parallel to NEW BC thru A 3) find tangent pt B on old IC.. wait, on a higher IC, B  4) new bundle C. A->B = SE, B->C = IE
- Hicks version uses same utility level instead (pivot + shift to old IC)

Slutsky Decompostion  (whiteboard, Tues)

Total Effect = Substituion Effect + Incorne Effect

Step 1: Orig1nal bundle A = (x1, x2) on budget line BL0
Step 2: Price of good 1 falls -> BL rotates outward, BL1
Step 3: Draw hypothetical line BL' parallel to BL1 passing thru A
   (gives consumer just enough income to buy A at new prices)
Step 4: Optimal bundle on BL' = B   =>  A to B is [unreadable]
Step 5: From B to C (final choice on BL1) = Income Effect

Note: SE always moves opposite to price for x1.
IE depends on goood type: normal -> +, inferior -> -

Slutsky eqn:  dx1/dp1  =  SE  -  x1 (dx1/dm)
Giffen if inferior AND |IE| > |SE|   (very rarc!)

transcript:
Okay, so, um, let's get started. Good morning, everybody. Hope you all had a decent weekend. I, uh, I saw the game on Saturday, and I will not be discussing it, my heart cannot take it. Anyway. So today we're going to talk about income and substitution effects, which is, um, really the heart of how we get from a single optimization problem to an actual demand curve.

So, here's the question. When the price of a good falls, why do you buy more of it? And you'd say, well, it's cheaper, duh. But there are actually two things going on, so, two separate reasons. Reason one, the good is now cheaper relative to other goods. So you substitute toward it. That's the substitution effect. Reason two, um, you're effectively richer. The same paycheck now buys more stuff. That's the income effect.

So let's do this on the board. We start with a budget line, and we've got our consumer at bundle A, where an indifference curve is tangent to the budget line. Now the price of good one drops, so the budget line pivots outward around the vertical intercept. Right? The vertical intercept doesn't move because the price of good two didn't change. Okay. So the new optimum is at C, on a higher indifference curve. The total change from A to C is the total effect.

Now, to split it up, we need a, um, a hypothetical. So we take the new price ratio, the slope of the new budget line, and we slide a line with that slope back down until it just touches, uh, well, in the Slutsky version, until it passes through the original bundle A. So the consumer could still afford A, but at the new relative prices. And then we ask, where would they choose on that line? Call that point B. The move from A to B is the substitution effect. Pure relative price change, no change in purchasing power. And then B to C is the income effect.

Now here's the key thing, and this will be on the exam: the substitution effect always goes in the opposite direction from the price change. Always. If the price falls, you buy more of that good through substitution. The income effect, though, depends on the type of good. For a normal good, income goes up effectively, you buy more, so the income effect reinforces the substitution effect. For an inferior good, so, think instant noodles, um, when you get richer you buy less, so the income effect pushes the opposite way.

So, uh, what if the income effect is negative and bigger than the substitution effect? Then you'd buy less of the good when its price falls. That's a Giffen good. Super rare. People argue about whether there are any real examples. There's a famous paper on rice in China, and, um, it's, let's say, contested.

We can write this algebraically. The Slutsky equation says the change in demand from a price change equals the substitution effect minus the quantity times the change in demand with respect to income. So the sign of that second piece is what matters. Okay, any questions on that? Yeah, in the back. Right, so the minus sign is because a price decrease acts like an income increase. Good question.

Alright, a couple of announcements before we go. Quiz 3, which was set for this Saturday, October 24th, is moving. Several of you pointed out it overlaps with the career fair weekend, and also we're a little behind. So the quiz will now close on Thursday, October 29th, at 11:59 pm. Same format, same material. And problem set 4 is still due next Tuesday. Okay? Great.

So for next time, read the section on the Slutsky equation and try the practice problem with the Cobb-Douglas example. Let's do one quick numeric example now, so everybody sees the steps before you leave. Say the consumer has income one hundred, price of good one goes from four to two, price of good two is five, and utility is x1 times x2. We'll find A first, then the compensated bundle B, then C. Pencils out, let's go.
